      "title": "Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be canceled when the request returns",
      "body": "In Create, the goroutine derives a 10-second context from the incoming request context with context.WithTimeoutCause. Because Create returns immediately, the HTTP request context is canceled when the request completes, canceling the child context and likely abortting Legacy.Create. The same pattern is used in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). This defeats the purpose of the asynchronous legacy safety write. Use a detached context, such as context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a background context carrying only needed values, plus the timeout."

      "severity": "high",
      "category": "concurrency",
      "title": "Fire-and-forget legacy writes are not ordered",
      "body": "All write operations start an independent goroutine to write to legacy and do not sequence those writes. Rapid create/update/delete requests for the same object can cause legacy operations to run out of order, for example update before create, delete before create, or create after delete. This can leave the legacy store inconsistent even though unified storage is correct. Since mode 3 is intended to keep legacy as a safe fallback, these writes need per-resource ordering or another synchronization mechanism."

      "severity": "high",

      "body": "Create launches Legacy.Create in a goroutine with the same obj that was passed to Storage.Create. If Storage.Create mutates obj or returns it as created, the API server may serialize the returned object concurrently while the goroutine reads or mutates the same runtime.Object in Legacy.Create. runtime.Object instances are not generally safe for concurrent use. Pass a deep copy to the asynchronous legacy write."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go",
      "line": 139,
      "severity": "high",
      "category": "data",
      "title": "Legacy update is recomputed from objInfo instead of mirroring the unified-storage result",
      "body": "In Update, after Storage.Update succeeds, the async Legacy.Update is called with the original rest.UpdatedObjectInfo. Legacy.Update will typically fetch the current legacy object and call UpdatedObject again, so the legacy object may be computed from divergent legacy state or from a request-scoped or non-idempotent UpdatedObjectInfo. The previous implementation precomputed the updated object and passed the unified result to legacy. The new code can write a different object to legacy than the one stored in unified storage. Pass an UpdatedObjectInfo that returns the object returned by Storage.Update, preferably a deep copy."
    },
    {

      "severity": "medium",

      "title": "Legacy delete is skipped when unified delete returns NotFound",
      "body": "Delete returns immediately for any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. The previous mode 3 behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted Legacy.Delete, allowing cleanup of stale legacy objects. With this change, an object that exists only in legacy will not be removed, leaving orphaned data in the legacy store even though the API returns NotFound."

      "line": 45,
      "severity": "medium",

      "title": "Storage failures are recorded as legacy duration metrics",
      "body": "In Create, when Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration with the storage start time. The same happens in Update at line 129. This attributes unified-storage latency and errors to the legacy store and fails to record a storage duration for the failed storage operation. Metrics and alerts for legacy and storage error rates will be incorrect."

      "title": "Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label",
      "body": "In Delete, the successful storage duration is recorded with name as the third argument, while other calls use the kind. If that metric argument is the kind label, this emits a per-resource-name label value. That breaks aggregation and can create high-cardinality metrics. Use the resource kind, not the object name."
    },

      "file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go",
      "line": 166,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "DeleteCollection records legacy async duration as a storage metric",
      "body": "In DeleteCollection's goroutine, after Legacy.DeleteCollection completes, the code calls recordStorageDuration. This records the legacy store's async duration and error state as if it were unified storage. Legacy failures will be invisible as legacy failures and storage metrics will be double-counted or incorrectly marked failed. This should call recordLegacyDuration."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go",
      "line": 97,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "Delete puts the wrong logger into the context",
      "body": "Delete builds log with name, kind, and method values, but then sets the context to klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of klog.NewContext(ctx, log). As a result, downstream logging from Storage.Delete and Legacy.Delete loses the request-specific fields, making debugging harder."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go",
      "line": 56,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged",
      "body": "The goroutines for Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection only record a metric when the legacy operation fails; they do not log the error or identify the affected object. Since the API returns success to the client even if the legacy safety write fails, operators have little information to detect or diagnose divergence. Add error logging for asynchronous legacy failures."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go",
      "line": 172,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "concurrency",
      "title": "Destroy does not wait for in-flight asynchronous legacy writes",
      "body": "DualWriterMode3.Destroy destroys both Storage and Legacy immediately, but write methods launch untracked goroutines that may still be using Legacy. On shutdown or mode change, those goroutines may fail or panic because the underlying storage has been closed. Track pending asynchronous writes and wait or cancel them during Destroy."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go",

      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "test_gap",
      "title": "Mode 3 unit tests do not synchronize or verify asynchronous legacy writes",
      "body": "TestMode3_Delete calls dw.Delete, which launches a goroutine to call Legacy.Delete, but the test neither sets a mock expectation for Legacy.Delete nor waits or asserts that it happened. DeleteCollection has the same issue, and Create/Update tests set legacy expectations but return without waiting or asserting that the asynchronous calls occurred. This makes the tests racy: they may pass before the goroutine runs, or an unexpected mock call may panic later. They also do not actually verify the mode 3 asynchronous legacy-write behavior."
    },
    {
      "file": "pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go",
      "line": 132,
      "severity": "medium",

      "title": "Mode 3 integration test races with asynchronous legacy writes",
      "body": "The added mode 3 subtest runs doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes objects through the k8s API and then immediately checks the legacy /api/playlists endpoints. In mode 3, writes to legacy are asynchronous fire-and-forget goroutines, so the legacy endpoints may not yet reflect the change. Without polling or waiting, the integration test is flaky and can pass or fail depending on goroutine scheduling."
    }

findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be canceled when the request returns
findings.body: In Create, the goroutine derives a 10-second context from the incoming request context with context.WithTimeoutCause. Because Create returns immediately, the HTTP request context is canceled when the request completes, canceling the child context and likely abortting Legacy.Create. The same pattern is used in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). This defeats the purpose of the asynchronous legacy safety write. Use a detached context, such as context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a background context carrying only needed values, plus the timeout.

findings.title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes are not ordered
findings.body: All write operations start an independent goroutine to write to legacy and do not sequence those writes. Rapid create/update/delete requests for the same object can cause legacy operations to run out of order, for example update before create, delete before create, or create after delete. This can leave the legacy store inconsistent even though unified storage is correct. Since mode 3 is intended to keep legacy as a safe fallback, these writes need per-resource ordering or another synchronization mechanism.

findings.title: Async legacy create may use the same runtime.Object that is returned to the client
findings.body: Create launches Legacy.Create in a goroutine with the same obj that was passed to Storage.Create. If Storage.Create mutates obj or returns it as created, the API server may serialize the returned object concurrently while the goroutine reads or mutates the same runtime.Object in Legacy.Create. runtime.Object instances are not generally safe for concurrent use. Pass a deep copy to the asynchronous legacy write.

findings.title: Legacy update is recomputed from objInfo instead of mirroring the unified-storage result
findings.body: In Update, after Storage.Update succeeds, the async Legacy.Update is called with the original rest.UpdatedObjectInfo. Legacy.Update will typically fetch the current legacy object and call UpdatedObject again, so the legacy object may be computed from divergent legacy state or from a request-scoped or non-idempotent UpdatedObjectInfo. The previous implementation precomputed the updated object and passed the unified result to legacy. The new code can write a different object to legacy than the one stored in unified storage. Pass an UpdatedObjectInfo that returns the object returned by Storage.Update, preferably a deep copy.

findings.title: Legacy delete is skipped when unified delete returns NotFound
findings.body: Delete returns immediately for any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. The previous mode 3 behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted Legacy.Delete, allowing cleanup of stale legacy objects. With this change, an object that exists only in legacy will not be removed, leaving orphaned data in the legacy store even though the API returns NotFound.

findings.title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy duration metrics
findings.body: In Create, when Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration with the storage start time. The same happens in Update at line 129. This attributes unified-storage latency and errors to the legacy store and fails to record a storage duration for the failed storage operation. Metrics and alerts for legacy and storage error rates will be incorrect.

findings.title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
findings.body: In Delete, the successful storage duration is recorded with name as the third argument, while other calls use the kind. If that metric argument is the kind label, this emits a per-resource-name label value. That breaks aggregation and can create high-cardinality metrics. Use the resource kind, not the object name.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records legacy async duration as a storage metric
findings.body: In DeleteCollection's goroutine, after Legacy.DeleteCollection completes, the code calls recordStorageDuration. This records the legacy store's async duration and error state as if it were unified storage. Legacy failures will be invisible as legacy failures and storage metrics will be double-counted or incorrectly marked failed. This should call recordLegacyDuration.

findings.title: Delete puts the wrong logger into the context
findings.body: Delete builds log with name, kind, and method values, but then sets the context to klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of klog.NewContext(ctx, log). As a result, downstream logging from Storage.Delete and Legacy.Delete loses the request-specific fields, making debugging harder.

findings.title: Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged
findings.body: The goroutines for Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection only record a metric when the legacy operation fails; they do not log the error or identify the affected object. Since the API returns success to the client even if the legacy safety write fails, operators have little information to detect or diagnose divergence. Add error logging for asynchronous legacy failures.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: DualWriterMode3.Destroy destroys both Storage and Legacy immediately, but write methods launch untracked goroutines that may still be using Legacy. On shutdown or mode change, those goroutines may fail or panic because the underlying storage has been closed. Track pending asynchronous writes and wait or cancel them during Destroy.

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests do not synchronize or verify asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: TestMode3_Delete calls dw.Delete, which launches a goroutine to call Legacy.Delete, but the test neither sets a mock expectation for Legacy.Delete nor waits or asserts that it happened. DeleteCollection has the same issue, and Create/Update tests set legacy expectations but return without waiting or asserting that the asynchronous calls occurred. This makes the tests racy: they may pass before the goroutine runs, or an unexpected mock call may panic later. They also do not actually verify the mode 3 asynchronous legacy-write behavior.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration test races with asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: The added mode 3 subtest runs doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes objects through the k8s API and then immediately checks the legacy /api/playlists endpoints. In mode 3, writes to legacy are asynchronous fire-and-forget goroutines, so the legacy endpoints may not yet reflect the change. Without polling or waiting, the integration test is flaky and can pass or fail depending on goroutine scheduling.
